t.6.92.1: But Rāvaṇa, who prided himself on his prowess in battle, being then wrathfully harassed in the fight by that Kākutstha, fell into a great rage.
t.6.92.2: His eyes blazing with fury, the mighty one drew back his bow and, utterly enraged, assailed Rāghava in that great battle.
t.6.92.3: Like a rain-cloud pouring from the sky, Rāvaṇa filled Rāghava with arrows, with thousands of streams of shafts, as one fills a pond.
t.6.92.4: Though covered in battle by a net of arrows released from the bow, Kākutstha, immovable like a great mountain, did not tremble.
t.6.92.5: Standing firm in battle and warding off the nets of arrows with his own arrows, that mighty one received them as if they were the rays of the sun.
t.6.92.6: Then the enraged night-ranger, swift of hand, struck thousands of arrows into the chest of the great-souled Rāghava.
t.6.92.7: Smeared all over with blood in battle, he, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, appeared like a mighty kiṃśuka tree in full bloom in the forest.
t.6.92.8: Enraged by the strike of the arrows, Kākutstha too, of exceedingly great splendor, took up arrows that blazed like the sun at the end of the age.
t.6.92.9: Then both of them, Rāma and Rāvaṇa, greatly enraged, could no longer make each other out in the battle, shrouded as it was in a darkness of arrows.
t.6.92.10: Then the heroic Rāma, son of Daśaratha, filled with wrath, laughed and spoke harsh words to Rāvaṇa.
t.6.92.11: O vilest of rākṣasas, since my helpless wife was carried off by you from Janasthāna without my knowledge, you are not truly valiant.
t.6.92.12: Having forcibly carried off Vaidehī, wretched and separated from me as she dwelt in the great forest, you think, "I am a hero."
t.6.92.13: O hero against helpless women who have no protector, O violator of other men's wives, having done a cowardly deed you think, 'I am a hero!'
t.6.92.14: O you who have broken every bound, shameless one, never steady in your conduct! Out of arrogance you have taken death upon yourself, and still you think, 'I am a hero.'
t.6.92.16: Now, today, reap the very great fruit of that deed which you committed out of arrogance, a deed contemptible and harmful.
t.6.92.15: A great deed, praiseworthy and glorious, has indeed been done by you, a hero, the brother of Dhanada, accompanied by your forces!
t.6.92.17: And you consider yourself a hero, O evil-minded one! Yet you feel no shame at all, you who carried off Sītā like a thief.
t.6.92.18: Had Sītā been seized by you by force in my presence, then, slain by my arrows, you would now be seeing your brother Khara.
t.6.92.19: By good fortune, O wicked-souled one, you have come within the range of my sight. Today with sharp arrows I shall lead you to the abode of Yama.
t.6.92.20: Today let the flesh-eating creatures drag away your head with its blazing earrings, severed by my arrows and flung down in the dust of the battlefield.
t.6.92.22: Today, when you lie fallen and lifeless, pierced by my arrows, let the birds drag out your entrails, as Garuḍas drag out serpents.
t.6.92.21: O Rāvaṇa, when you have been hurled down upon the earth, let the vultures, swooping onto your chest, thirstily drink the blood that wells up from among the arrowheads lodged in you.
t.6.92.23: Speaking thus, the heroic Rāma, destroyer of foes, covered the lord of the Rākṣasas, who stood close by, with showers of arrows.
t.6.92.24: In that battle the valour, strength and joy of Rāma, who longed for the death of his enemy, became twofold, and so too did the power of his weapons.
t.6.92.25: All the weapons manifested themselves to him whose mind was well known to itself, and out of great joy the immensely powerful one became even swifter of hand.
t.6.92.26: Perceiving these auspicious signs occurring in himself, Rāma, the destroyer of rākṣasas, tormented Rāvaṇa all the more.
t.6.92.27: Struck by the showers of stones from the monkeys and by the rain of arrows from Rāghava, Daśagrīva became one whose heart was reeling.
t.6.92.29: Even the arrows he discharged and his many kinds of weapons do not serve the purpose of battle for one upon whom the hour of death is advancing.
t.6.92.28: And when, his inner self distraught, he neither took up a weapon nor drew his bow, nor made any answer to his opponent's valor...
t.6.92.30: But his charioteer, the driver of his chariot, seeing him in that state, calmly and without alarm slowly drove his chariot away from the battle.
